overview.title: Student & Teacher Overview: Lesson 21
overview.pill: Using Functions and Graphs to Solve Problems
overview.text: Students have spent several lessons in this module studying linear and exponential functions. This lesson has students compare and contrast the two functions to solidify their understanding of each. Students then learn how to differentiate between the two functions by recognizing a constant rate of change or a common quotient in data tables or by recognizing the features in their graphs or formulas.
outcomes: Students create models and understand the differences between linear and exponential models that are represented in different ways.
overview.teacherInsight: Emphasize precise mathematical definitions and multiple problem-solving representations. Encourage students to check the reasonableness of their numerical solutions.

vocabulary.definition: If students are struggling with the type of function, have them plot the points.

exitTicket.title: Lesson 21 Exit Ticket: Comparing Linear and Exponential Models Again
exitTicket.prompt:
Exit Ticket

Here is a classic riddle: Mr. Smith has an apple orchard. He hires his daughter, Lucy, to pick apples and offers her two payment options:

Option A: $1.50 per bushel of apples picked

Option B: 1 cent for picking one bushel, 3 cents for picking two bushels, 9 cents for picking three bushels, and so on, with the amount of money tripling for each additional bushel picked

Write a function to model each option.

If Lucy picks six bushels of apples, which option should she choose?

If Lucy picks 12 bushels of apples, which option should she choose?

How many bushels of apples does Lucy need to pick to make Option B better for her than Option A?
exitTicket.solution:
Here is a classic riddle: Mr. Smith has an apple orchard. He hires his daughter, Lucy, to pick apples and offers her two payment options::

Option A: $1.50 per bushel of apples picked

Option B: 1 cent for picking one bushel, 3 cents for picking two bushels, 9 cents for picking three bushels, and so on, with the amount of money tripling for each additional bushel picked

Write a function to model each option.

Option A: f(x)=1.50x, where x is the number of bushels of apples picked

Option B: g(x)=0.01(3)^{x-1}, where x is the number of bushels of apples picked

If Lucy picks six bushels of apples, which option should she choose?

Option A: $9Option B: $2.43Option A is better.

If Lucy picks 12 bushels of apples, which option should she choose?

Option A: $18Option B: $1,771.47Option B is much better.

How many bushels of apples does Lucy need to pick to make Option B better for her than Option A?

The eighth bushel picked is when the exponential function exceeds the linear function.

problemSet.title: Official Worksheet: Problem Set & Practice
problemSet.description: Master Comparing Linear and Exponential Models Again through authentic curriculum practice problems. Check your work using the expandable teacher solution key below.

problems.prompt: For each table in Problems 1—6, classify the data as describing a linear relationship, an exponential growth relationship, an exponential decay relationship, or neither. If the relationship is linear, calculate the constant rate of change (slope), and write a formula for the linear function that models the data. If the function is exponential, calculate the common quotient for input values that are distance one apart, and write the formula for the exponential function that models the data. For each linear or exponential function found, graph the equation y=f(x).

Here is a variation on a classic riddle: Jayden has a dog-walking business. He has two plans. Plan 1 includes walking a dog once a day for a rate of $5 per day. Plan 2 also includes one walk a day but charges 1 cent for 1 day, 2 cents for 2 days, 4 cents for 3 days, and 8 cents for 4 days and continues to double for each additional day. Mrs. Maroney needs Jayden to walk her dog every day for two weeks. Which plan should she choose? Show the work to justify your answer.
problems.solution:
Plan 1: 5\times 14=70 She will pay $70 for two weeks under Plan 1.

Plan 2: The price can be modeled using the function f(x)=0.01(2)^{x-1}, which describes the amount she pays for x days. Then,

f(14)=0.01(2)^{14-1} or f(14)=81.92.

She will pay $81.92 under Plan 2 for two weeks.

Plan 1 is the better choice.

problems.prompt:
Tim deposits money in a certificate of deposit account. The balance (in dollars) in his account t years after making the deposit is given by T(t)=1000(1.06)^{t} for t≥0.

Explain, in terms of the structure of the expression used to define T(t), why Tim's balance can never be $999.
problems.solution: (1.06)^{0}=1, and positive powers of 1.06 are larger than 1; thus, the minimum value T(t) attains, if t≥0, is 1,000. In the context given, a CD account grows in value over time, so with a deposit of $1,000, the value will never drop to $999.

problems.prompt: By what percent does the value of T(t) grow each year? Explain by writing a recursive formula for the sequence T(1), T(2), T(3), etc.
problems.solution:
Writing out the sequence, we see:

Year 1: 1000(1.06)^{1}Year 2: 1000(1.06)^{2}Year 3: 1000(1.06)^{3}

Thus, T(n+1)=T(n)(1.06) or T(n+1)=T(n)+T(n)(0.06), showing that T(n) grows by 6% per year.

By what percentage does the value of T(t) grow every two years? (Hint: Use your recursive formula to write T(n+2) in terms of T(n).)

Since, T(n+1)=T(n)(1.06), we can write:

T(n+2)=T(n+1)(1.06)=T(n)(1.06)(1.06),

or T(n+2)=T(n)(1.1236).

Hence, the amount in his account grows by 12.36% every two years.

problems.prompt:
Your mathematics teacher asks you to sketch a graph of the exponential function f(x)=(\frac{3}{2})^{x} for x, a number between 0 and 40 inclusively, using a scale of 10 units to one inch for both the x- and y-axes.

What are the dimensions (in feet) of the roll of paper needed to sketch this graph?
problems.solution: The roll would need to be a bit wider than 4 in. (\frac{1}{3} ft. ) and, after rounding up, about 1,105,734 in. (or 92,145 ft. long).

problems.prompt: How many more feet of paper would you need to add to the roll in order to graph the function on the interval 0≤x≤41?
problems.solution: It would require approximately 46,072 more feet of paper. Teachers: Look for the easy solution, which is f(41)=f(40)\times 1.5=f(40)+f(40)\times \frac{1}{2}.

problems.prompt: Find an m so that the linear function g(x)=mx+2 is greater than f(x) for all x such that 0≤x≤40, but f(41)>g(41).
problems.solution: There are many possible answers: Any number between (roughly) 276,433.275 and 404,536 will do. Note that f(40)≈11 057 332.32 and f(41)≈16 585 998.48, so any slope such that 11 057 333≤g(40) and g(41)≤16 585 998 will do. Since g(40)=40m+2, solving 11 057 333=40m+2 or m=276 433.275 might produce such a linear function. We need to check only that the function g(x)=276 433.275x+2 satisfies f(41)>g(41), which it does because g(41)=11 333 766.275.
